title: Snakebite
summary: Treat as a medical emergency: keep the person completely still and transport without walking.
sources: World Health Organization — Snakebite envenoming and Guidelines for the Management of Snakebites
2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid — Snakebite
actions: Move to a safe distance from the snake and call emergency services. Do not approach, catch, or kill it.
Reassure the person and keep the whole body still. Do not allow walking. Remove rings, watches, tight footwear, and tight clothing before swelling.
Immobilize the bitten limb in a comfortable position with a simple splint that does not impair circulation. Arrange carried transport.
Record the time and progression of swelling. Describe the snake only if it was seen safely.
Monitor breathing, alertness, unusual bleeding, drooping eyelids, weakness, vomiting, and spreading swelling. Start CPR if normal breathing stops.
Pressure-immobilization bandaging is species- and region-specific; use it only when a local protocol or emergency dispatcher directs it.
prohibitions: Do not cut, puncture, burn, or suck the wound.
Do not apply a tight tourniquet or constricting band.
Do not apply ice, electric shock, herbs, or chemicals.
Do not give alcohol or make the person walk.

regionalNotes.IR: In Iran, medically important vipers include Echis carinatus and Macrovipera lebetina. Razi polyvalent antivenom is used in clinical settings. Species identification and antivenom selection are not first-aid tasks; emergency services should direct transport.

redFlags.text: Emergency warning signs selected—contact emergency services now.

emergencyCall.text: Any known or suspected venomous snakebite requires immediate emergency assessment; do not wait for symptoms.
